propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the RAD decision upholding the RPD's rejection of his refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board, which upheld the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the RAD decision upholding the RPD's rejection of his refugee claim, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD made no reviewable error on credibility or new evidence admission; judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not established that the RAD made a reviewable error in confirming the rejection of his claim on credibility grounds. The RAD also reasonably refused to admit his proposed new evidence. Accordingly, this application for judicial review is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reviewable error by the RAD and dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: Applicant arrived in Canada on visitor visa August 23, 2023, and claimed refugee protection November 3, 2023.
propositions.quote: On August 23, 2023, the Applicant arrived in Canada on a visitor visa and, on November 3, 2023, claimed refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant arrived in Canada August 23, 2023, and claimed refugee protection November 3, 2023.

propositions.text: Applicant's refugee claim is based on fear of harm in Liberia from traditional elders and Chief Zoe of Gayelahdee clan.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s refugee claim is based on an alleged fear of harm in Liberia at the hands of traditional elders and the Chief Zoe of the Gayelahdee clan.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant fears harm in Liberia from traditional elders and Chief Zoe of the Gayelahdee clan.

propositions.text: Applicant alleged being ordained Christian minister; refused ancestral role as 'country devil' due to faith; fled after threats.
propositions.quote: In his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, the Applicant alleged being an ordained Christian minister. In December 2022, he and his wife traveled from Monrovia to his hometown to visit his ailing father. The Chief Zoe and elders demanded that, as the first male child, he take over his father’s ancestral role as “country devil”. The Applicant refused because of his Christian faith. Following threats against their lives, the Applicant and his wife returned to Monrovia.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts the Applicant's claim of refusing ancestral role due to Christian faith and fleeing after threats.

propositions.text: Applicant traveled to Canada August 2023 for church conference; elders threatened family October 9, 2023; police rescued family.
propositions.quote: In August 2023, the Applicant traveled to Canada on a visitor visa to attend a pastoral church conference. He alleged that, on October 9, 2023, a group of elders and Chief Zoes showed up at his family residence in Monrovia, threatening to kidnap his wife and children. The Applicant’s wife contacted a pastor friend, Pastor James, who arrived with police officers to rescue the family and take them into hiding.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant traveled to Canada August 2023; elders threatened family October 9, 2023; police rescued them.

propositions.text: RPD rejected claim October 24, 2024, finding Applicant not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection due to lack of credible evidence.
propositions.quote: On October 24, 2024, the RPD rejected the claim, holding that the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, as he failed to adduce sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to establish his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the Applicant's claim October 24, 2024, for lack of credible evidence, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant appealed RPD decision to RAD November 3, 2024, represented by new counsel.
propositions.quote: On November 3, 2024, represented by new counsel, the Applicant appealed the RPD’s decision before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD November 3, 2024, with new counsel.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed appeal April 3, 2025, confirming RPD's decision and finding Applicant not credible on central allegations.
propositions.quote: On April 3, 2025, the RAD dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD’s decision, holding that the Applicant “is not credible regarding the central allegations of his claim”.

propositions.text: RAD refused to admit three new affidavits from Applicant's relatives as they could have been submitted earlier with due diligence.
propositions.quote: The RAD refused to admit three new affidavits sought to be adduced by the Applicant, from his “half-brother”, his uncle, and his mother. Although the affidavits were signed after the RPD decision, they described events that occurred before the RPD hearing and could have been submitted earlier with due diligence;

propositions.text: Even if admitted, affidavits lacked credibility due to source and lack of identity verification.
propositions.quote: Even if the RAD admitted the affidavits as new evidence, it would still not have found them credible given their source. Also, the affiants did not provide copies of identity cards, leaving the panel unable to verify their identities on a balance of probabilities;

propositions.text: RPD erred by accepting some evidence but denying credible evidence overall; error not serious enough to undermine decision as Applicant not credible on central claims.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in concluding, on one hand, that “there is no credible evidence relevant to [the Applicant’s] claim”, while accepting, on the other hand, that he was approached in his village to take over his father’s role as a traditional leader. However, this error was not “serious enough to undermine the overall correctness of [the RPD’s] decision”, as the Applicant is not credible with respect to central allegations of his claim;

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant failed to prove he is sole heir to 'country devil' role and did not disclose half-brother Jeremiah in BOC.
propositions.quote: Conducting its own review, the RAD found that the Applicant failed to establish that he is the only one to whom the position of “country devil” can be transmitted and that his brother Jeremiah would not be similarly targeted because he is his half-brother on his mother’s side. In his BOC form, he omitted to mention that Jeremiah was a half-brother. He also did not persuade the RAD that his Jeremiah was carrying the Mahn family name “simply because he chose to do so”;

propositions.text: RAD drew negative credibility inference from contradictions about Applicant's status as first male child and biological son compared to brother Jeremiah.
propositions.quote: Additionally, the RAD drew a negative credibility inference because the Applicant’s oral testimony, in which he claimed he was chosen because he is his father’s only biological male child, contradicted his statement in his BOC narrative that he was chosen for being the “first male child”, a claim further undermined by his oral admission that his brother Jeremiah is older than he is;

propositions.text: RAD drew negative inference from Applicant's failure to provide evidence about brother Jeremiah or explain lack of contact, rejecting his explanation.
propositions.quote: The RAD drew a further negative credibility inference from the Applicant’s failure to provide evidence on the circumstances of his brother Jeremiah or why he was not targeted, rejecting his explanation that he was no longer in touch with him, because the Applicant had successfully maintained contact with other family members and obtained documents from Liberia;

propositions.text: RAD did not accept news article photo of masked 'country devil' as linked to Applicant's father due to different counties.
propositions.quote: The RAD held that a news article featuring a photo of a masked “country devil” in Gbarpolu County could not be reliably linked to the Applicant’s father in Nimba County;

propositions.text: RAD did not accept Applicant's testimony that uncle led elders to Monrovia home, as uncle was not mentioned in BOC narrative.
propositions.quote: The RAD further did not accept the Applicant’s testimony on how the elders found his Monrovia home. Despite testifying at the hearing that his uncle led the traditional elders to his Monrovia residence, the Applicant failed to mention his uncle in his BOC narrative;

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismissed the appeal April 3, 2025, finding Applicant not credible and refusing new affidavits for lack of diligence and credibility, says the court.

propositions.text: Two issues: Was RAD unreasonable refusing new evidence? Was RAD unreasonable confirming RPD's rejection on credibility?
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review raises the following two issues: a)Was it unreasonable for the Refugee Appeal Division to refuse to admit the Applicant’s proposed new evidence? b)Was it unreasonable for the Refugee Appeal Division to dismiss the Applicant’s appeal and confirm the RPD’s rejection of the Applicant’s refugee claim based on his absence of credibility?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two issues: reasonableness of RAD refusing new evidence and confirming rejection on credibility.

propositions.text: Court applies reasonableness standard to RAD decisions on credibility and new evidence admission.
propositions.quote: This Court applies the reasonableness standard of review when reviewing the merits of a RAD decision. This includes the RAD’s conclusions related to a claimant’s credibility (Bamidele v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 999 at para 15) and the admission of new evidence on appeal (Bhuiyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 616 at para 50).

paragraphs.summary: The court states it applies reasonableness standard to RAD decisions on credibility and new evidence admission.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires decision to be internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: In applying the reasonableness standard of review, the role of a reviewing court is to examine the reasons given by the administrative decision maker and to determine whether the decision is based on “an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 85 [Vavilov]).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review requires coherent, rational, justified decision per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility; flaws must be central to render decision unreasonable (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: When assessing a decision on judicial review, the Court must determine whether the decision at issue bears the hallmarks of reasonableness, namely justification, transparency and intelligibility (Vavilov at para 99). Any flaws relied upon by the party challenging the decision must be “sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility; flaws must be significant (Vavilov).

propositions.text: Court is not convinced RAD erred in refusing to admit Applicant's proposed new evidence.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, I am not convinced the RAD made any reviewable error in refusing to admit the Applicant’s proposed new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not convinced the RAD erred in refusing to admit the Applicant's new evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant must establish admissibility of new evidence under IRPA s 110(4) criteria: arose after decision, not reasonably available, or could not reasonably be presented earlier.
propositions.quote: The onus was on the Applicant to establish that the proposed new evidence was admissible pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA), which requires an appellant to show that (i) the evidence arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) the evidence was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) the appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it to the RPD at the time of the decision (Figueroa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 521 at para 19).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant must meet IRPA s 110(4) criteria to admit new evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: RAD must strictly apply IRPA s 110(4) criteria and cannot disregard them (Singh).
propositions.quote: The RAD is strictly bound to apply the test set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and has no discretion to disregard the explicit criteria set out therein (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Singh, 2016 FCA 96 at para 63 [Singh]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must strictly apply IRPA s 110(4) criteria without discretion (Singh).

propositions.text: Raza criteria (credibility, relevance, newness, materiality) apply to IRPA s 110(4) evidence admission (Singh, Raza).
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal further held that the Raza criteria, developed for pre-removal risk assessments, also apply to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Accordingly, before admitting evidence under subsection 110(4), the RAD must also assess its credibility, relevance, newness and materiality (Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 at para 13; Singh at para 49).

paragraphs.summary: The court states Raza criteria apply to IRPA s 110(4) evidence admission (Singh, Raza).

propositions.text: Claimant must present all available evidence to RPD; cannot submit new evidence due to surprise at RPD decision (Thuraisingam, Abdullahi, Desalegn).
propositions.quote: A claimant is required to put their best foot forward before the RPD and present all the evidence that is available at the time (Thuraisingam v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1332 at para 10; Abdullahi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 260 at para 14). This means that a claimant is not entitled to submit new evidence “every time he or she is surprised by the RPD’s decision” (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Desalegn, 2016 FC 12 at para 23).

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimants must present all evidence to RPD and cannot submit new evidence just because surprised by RPD decision.

propositions.text: Evidence that only corroborates, contradicts, or clarifies RPD evidence is not 'new evidence' under IRPA s 110(4) (Singh).
propositions.quote: Thus, evidence that simply “corroborates facts, contradicts the RPD’s findings, or clarifies the evidence before the RPD”, does not qualify as “new evidence” under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA (Singh at para 50). Put simply, it is not the role of the RAD “to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD” (Singh at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: The court states evidence merely corroborating or contradicting RPD evidence is not new evidence under IRPA s 110(4).

propositions.text: RAD reasonably concluded Applicant's documents did not meet IRPA s 110(4) test for new evidence admission.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the RAD reasonably concluded that the documents sought to be adduced by the Applicant did not meet the test for admission of new evidence on appeal under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably concluded the Applicant's documents did not meet the test for new evidence admission under IRPA s 110(4).

propositions.text: RAD noted affidavits post-dated RPD decision but related to events before it
propositions.quote: the RAD did not dispute that the Applicant’s proposed new affidavits post-dated the RPD decision, it noted the allegations in these affidavits pertained to events that took place before the RPD decision

propositions.text: Applicant did not explain why affidavits were not available earlier or why he could not submit them before RPD
propositions.quote: the Applicant “[…] did not explain on appeal why these exhibits were not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or why the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring them to the RPD before the decision”

propositions.text: Applicant had three months between hearing and RPD decision to submit evidence
propositions.quote: Applicant had a three-month window between the hearing and the issuance of the RPD’s decision to obtain and submit corroborating evidence if he wished to do so

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's affidavits post-dated the RPD decision but related to prior events, and he did not explain why they were not submitted earlier despite a three-month window.

propositions.text: RAD rejected Applicant's argument that documents arose as direct response to RPD findings and could not be presented earlier
propositions.quote: The RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant’s argument that the documents “arose as a direct response to the RPD’s findings” and could not, for this reason, have been presented earlier

propositions.text: Documents addressed issues the RPD had identified as raising credibility concerns
propositions.quote: the documents seek to address issues that the RPD expressly canvassed the hearing as raising credibility concerns

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant's claim that documents arose as a direct response to RPD findings and noted they addressed issues already raised as credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RPD did not question Jeremiah's status as half-brother, so affidavit from half-brother should be admitted
propositions.quote: He therefore justifies the admission of the proposed affidavit from his “half-brother” on the basis that the RPD’s credibility concerns could not have been reasonably anticipated

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RPD did not question Jeremiah's half-brother status, justifying admission of the half-brother's affidavit.

propositions.text: Member questioned Applicant about Jeremiah's surname and eligibility to be 'country devil', putting Applicant on notice these were live issues
propositions.quote: these lines of questioning from the Member clearly put the Applicant on notice that Jeremiah’s lineage and ineligibility to become “country devil” were live issues

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD Member's questioning clearly put the Applicant on notice about Jeremiah's lineage and eligibility issues.

propositions.text: Credibility is always at issue in refugee hearings (Talukder v Canada)
propositions.quote: credibility is always in issue in refugee hearings (Talukder v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 668 at para 20)

propositions.text: RPD's credibility concerns arose from discrepancies and omissions in Applicant's own narrative and testimony
propositions.quote: the RPD’s credibility concerns arose directly from the material discrepancies and omissions in the Applicant’s own BOC narrative and oral testimony

propositions.text: Applicant cannot reasonably argue RPD's credibility findings were not foreseeable
propositions.quote: The Applicant therefore cannot reasonably argue that the RPD’s credibility findings could not have been anticipated

paragraphs.summary: The court notes credibility is always at issue; RPD's concerns arose from Applicant's discrepancies, so findings were foreseeable.

propositions.text: No unreasonableness found in RAD's exclusion of Applicant's affidavits
propositions.quote: I find nothing unreasonable in how the RAD evaluated and chose to exclude the Applicant’s proposed affidavits

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's exclusion of the Applicant's affidavits was reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant's arguments on new evidence admissibility under IRPA s.110(4) disposed; no need to address alternative Raza factors argument
propositions.quote: I do not need to address his alternative argument challenging the RAD’s finding that the affidavits failed to satisfy the Raza factors

paragraphs.summary: The court disposes of Applicant's new evidence admissibility arguments and declines to address alternative Raza factors argument.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably confirmed RPD's finding that Applicant was not credible on central claim allegations
propositions.quote: I am also of the view that the RAD acted reasonably in confirming the RPD’s finding that the Applicant was not credible regarding the central allegations of his claim

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably confirmed the RPD's non-credibility finding on the Applicant's central allegations.

propositions.text: RAD highlighted credibility problems including inconsistencies and omissions in Applicant's narrative and testimony
propositions.quote: The RAD highlighted several credibility problems, including various inconsistencies and omissions, arising from the Applicant’s BOC narrative and oral testimony

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found several credibility problems in the Applicant's narrative and testimony.

propositions.text: RAD assigned low probative value to Applicant's documentary evidence
propositions.quote: the RAD assigned low probative value to the documentary evidence the Applicant submitted as part of his claim

paragraphs.summary: The RAD gave low probative value to the Applicant's documentary evidence.

propositions.text: RAD found National Documentation Package did not support Applicant's alleged risk of abduction and mistreatment
propositions.quote: the RAD concluded that the objective evidence contained in the National Documentation Package related to Liberia did not support the Applicant’s alleged risk of abduction and mistreatment in Monrovia

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concluded objective evidence did not support the Applicant's alleged risk in Monrovia.

propositions.text: Court will address each of these points in turn
propositions.quote: I now address each of these points in turn

paragraphs.summary: The court states it will address each of the RAD's points in turn.

propositions.text: RAD's credibility analysis focused on three key aspects: country devil succession, news article figure, uncle directing pursuers
propositions.quote: The RAD’s credibility analysis focused on three key aspects of the Applicant’s claim: first, his claim that...; second, his attempt to link...; and third, his assertion that his uncle directed the pursuers

paragraphs.summary: The RAD focused credibility analysis on three key claim aspects: succession, news article figure, and uncle's role.

propositions.text: Applicant claimed brother Jeremiah was half-brother and ineligible to succeed as country devil, so not targeted
propositions.quote: the Applicant alleged that his brother Jeremiah was his “half-brother” on the maternal side... he would not be similarly targeted by traditionalists

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claimed Jeremiah was half-brother and thus ineligible to succeed as country devil, avoiding targeting.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found Applicant failed to prove Jeremiah's half-brother status with sufficient evidence
propositions.quote: The RAD reasonably determined that the Applicant failed to establish with sufficient and persuasive evidence the status of Jeremiah as his “half-brother”

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reasonably found Applicant failed to prove Jeremiah's half-brother status.

propositions.text: Applicant listed Jeremiah as brother with same last name, did not indicate half-brother in BOC form
propositions.quote: in his BOC form, the applicant listed Jeremiah as his “brother” and they share the same last name... Nowhere in the BOC form did the applicant refer to Jeremiah as his “half-brother”

paragraphs.summary: Applicant listed Jeremiah as brother with same last name, not as half-brother, in BOC form.

propositions.text: Applicant called himself only biological male child orally but 'first' male child in BOC, undermined by brother's older age
propositions.quote: applicant referred to himself as his father’s “only biological male child” during oral testimony, whereas he referred to himself as the “first” male child in the BOC form

paragraphs.summary: Applicant inconsistently described himself as only biological male child orally but first male child in BOC form.

propositions.text: RAD agreed with RPD's negative credibility inference from Applicant's failure to provide evidence on Jeremiah or why not targeted
propositions.quote: RAD could reasonably agree with the RPD’s decision to draw a negative credibility inference from the Applicant’s failure to provide any evidence on the circumstances of his brother Jeremiah or why he was not targeted by the elders

propositions.text: Applicant maintained contact with other family and obtained documents despite no contact with Jeremiah
propositions.quote: Applicant successfully maintained contact with other family members and obtained documents from Liberia

paragraphs.summary: RAD agreed with RPD's negative credibility inference due to Applicant's failure to explain Jeremiah's circumstances despite other contacts.

propositions.text: Presumption of truthfulness attaches to claimant testimony (Maldonado)
propositions.quote: a presumption of truthfulness attaches to a claimant’s testimony (Maldonado v Canada)

propositions.text: Claimants generally not required to provide corroborating evidence (Senadheerage)
propositions.quote: claimants are generally not required to provide corroborating evidence (Senadheerage)

propositions.text: RAD can draw negative credibility inference if claimant lacks effort to obtain corroboration when credibility is questioned and evidence expected (Senadheerage, Lawani)
propositions.quote: RAD can draw a negative credibility inference based on the claimant’s lack of effort to obtain corroborative evidence, when there is already a valid reason to question a claimant’s credibility...

paragraphs.summary: Presumption of truthfulness applies, but RAD may infer negative credibility if claimant fails to seek corroboration when expected and credibility questioned.

propositions.text: RAD rejected Applicant's claim that masked figure in news article was his father due to lack of evidence and different location
propositions.quote: RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant’s assertion that his father was represented in a news article showing a picture of a masked, unidentifiable figure

paragraphs.summary: RAD rejected Applicant's claim that masked figure in news article was his father due to lack of evidence and location mismatch.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably concluded the Applicant's testimony on the photograph's origin lacked plausibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD also reasonably concluded that the Applicant’s testimony regarding how the photograph was obtained lacked plausibility.

propositions.text: It was improbable the Applicant's wife would invite a stranger from Nimba into her safe house to hand-deliver a public photograph.
propositions.quote: It was indeed improbable that his wife, living in strict concealment in Monrovia due to her fear of Nimba traditionalists, would invite a stranger from Nimba into her safe house merely to hand-deliver a publicly accessible photograph

propositions.text: The RAD may base credibility conclusions on implausibilities, common sense and rationality (Lawani v Canada).
propositions.quote: The RAD may draw conclusions concerning an appellant’s credibility based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality (Lawani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 924 at para 26 [Lawani]).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably disbelieved the Applicant's testimony about the photograph's origin, citing implausibility and Lawani precedent.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably dismissed the Applicant's belated testimony about his uncle, which was omitted from his initial narrative.
propositions.quote: Finally, on the third central issue, the RAD reasonably dismissed the Applicant’s belated testimony about his uncle.

propositions.text: Applicant's BOC narrative omitted mention of his uncle, only stating elders and Chief Zoes visited his residence.
propositions.quote: In his BOC narrative, the Applicant omitted any mention of his uncle, stating simply that the elders and Chief Zoes paid a visit to his Monrovia residence.

propositions.text: Applicant first testified at hearing that his uncle led elders to his home when asked how pursuers found his address.
propositions.quote: when pressed at the hearing to explain how pursuers from a remote village could locate his family’s specific address in a metropolitan city like Monrovia, the Applicant testified for the first time that his uncle had led the elders to his home

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably dismissed the Applicant's late testimony about his uncle, omitted from his initial narrative but introduced at hearing.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably concluded the Applicant amended his story to fill a narrative gap about his uncle's betrayal.
propositions.quote: the RAD acted reasonably in concluding that the Applicant amended his story in order to resolve a gap in his narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably concluded the Applicant changed his story to fill a gap about his uncle's betrayal.

propositions.text: The RAD erred in stating the RPD found the claim 'manifestly unfounded'.
propositions.quote: the Applicant also submits that the RAD erred in stating that the RPD had found his claim to be “manifestly unfounded”

propositions.text: The RAD's error on 'manifestly unfounded' is not determinative as the RAD conducted a full independent merits assessment.
propositions.quote: this error is not determinative. Because the RAD conducted a full, independent assessment of the merits, the Applicant suffered no prejudice, and this oversight alone does not vitiate the RAD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD erred on 'manifestly unfounded' but the court finds this error harmless as the RAD fully assessed the merits.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably assessed the documentary evidence submitted by the Applicant.
propositions.quote: I am also of the view that the RAD reasonably assessed the documentary evidence submitted by the Applicant in support of his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD reasonably assessed the Applicant's documentary evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD must base decisions on evidence considered credible or trustworthy under IRPA subsection 171(a.3).
propositions.quote: Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD is mandated to base its decisions on evidence considered “credible or trustworthy in the circumstances” (subsection 171(a.3) of the IRPA).

propositions.text: Numerous problems undermined the weight of the Applicant's documentary materials.
propositions.quote: there were numerous problems that undermined the weight to be given to the Applicant’s materials.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the RAD must rely on credible evidence and found many problems with the Applicant's documentary materials.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably found the Applicant's wife's written communications had low probative value.
propositions.quote: the RAD reasonably concluded that the written communications from the Applicant’s wife carried low probative value

propositions.text: The October 9, 2023 email omitted any mention of a kidnapping threat despite agents visiting the family home that day.
propositions.quote: The email of October 9, 2023, which was sent the exact day the agents of persecution visited the family home, completely omitted any reference to a threat of kidnapping.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably gave low weight to the Applicant's wife's communications, noting an October 9 email omitted kidnapping threats.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably found it implausible the wife omitted a central kidnapping threat in the October 9 email.
propositions.quote: The RAD could reasonably find it implausible that the Applicant’s wife would omit a threat as central and severe as the abduction of her children.

propositions.text: The July 2, 2024 letter surfaced the kidnapping allegation months later and referred to the wife in third person, casting doubt on authorship.
propositions.quote: This critical allegation only surfaced months later in her subsequent letter of July 2, 2024. Further, even though it was supposedly written by the Applicant’s wife, the letter referred to her in the third person (“his wife and children”), legitimately casting doubt on whether she was indeed the letter’s true author.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably doubted the wife's omission of kidnapping threats and questioned the July 2 letter's authorship.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably concluded the Special Investigations Unit report was not genuine due to wording mirroring a separate letter.
propositions.quote: the RAD acted reasonably in concluding, on a balance of probabilities, that the investigation report from the Office of the Special Investigations Unit was not a genuine document. A key passage in this official report closely mirrored the wording of a separate letter from the Global Revival Center.

propositions.text: The RAD drew negative inferences from the report's wording and conclusion that police cannot act, recommending hiding and refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the RAD was justified in drawing a negative inference regarding the authenticity of the report based on this identical wording. Further, the RAD could draw a negative inference from the fact that the report is a written in a way that concludes that the police cannot do anything about the threats faced by the Applicant. Indeed, the report concludes with a “recommendation” that the Applicant’s wife and children remain in hiding, and that the Applicant seek refugee, while the police complete its investigation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably doubted the authenticity of the police report due to wording and conclusions recommending hiding and refugee claim.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably assigned low probative value to the Global Revival Center letter due to similarity to police report and lack of source explanation.
propositions.quote: the RAD reasonably chose to assign the document low probative value because it contained language that was similar to that found in the police report, undermining its authenticity. Also, the letter did not indicate how its authors, who are church administrators located in Monrovia, obtained knowledge of the specific threats made against the Applicant on October 9, 2023

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably gave low weight to the Global Revival Center letter due to similarity to police report and unclear source of knowledge.

propositions.text: The RAD reasonably determined the Applicant's forward-looking risk allegations were unsupported by objective country condition evidence.
propositions.quote: Finally, the RAD reasonably determined that the Applicant’s allegations of forward-looking risk in Monrovia were not supported by the objective evidence on country conditions set out in the National Documentation Package regarding Liberia

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably rejected the Applicant's forward-looking risk claims as unsupported by country evidence.

propositions.text: The UN report documents Poro society forceful initiations but no abduction or mistreatment in Monrovia.
propositions.quote: while the UN Mission in Liberia report documents instances of Poro society members forcefully initiating individuals who transgress traditional rules, it does not document any instances of abduction or mistreatment occurring in the capital city of Monrovia

propositions.text: Objective documentation confirms the issue is mainly rural; a trial was moved to Monrovia to avoid juror bias.
propositions.quote: The RAD also noted that the objective documentation submitted by the Applicant himself confirmed that the issue is predominantly one of rural communities, given that the article reported that a trial was transferred from a rural county to Monrovia to avoid juror bias

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably noted the UN report shows no abduction in Monrovia and the issue is mainly rural.

propositions.text: The court is satisfied the RAD's decision was reasonable and supported by logical reasons.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the RAD’s decision was reasonable. The outcome is supported by reasons which are logical and rational.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD's decision was reasonable and logically supported.

propositions.text: It was reasonably open to the RAD to find the Applicant not credible and dismiss the appeal, confirming the RPD's decision.
propositions.quote: it was reasonably open to the RAD to conclude that the RPD was correct that the Appellant is not credible regarding the central allegations to his claim and, on that basis, dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD reasonably dismissed the appeal and confirmed the RPD's decision due to Applicant's lack of credibility.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the RAD failed to apply the presumption of credibility and made no explicit finding it was rebutted.
propositions.quote: the Applicant devoted a substantial portion of both his written and oral arguments to the position that the RAD failed to apply the “presumption of credibility” and made no explicit finding that it was rebutted.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD failed to apply or explicitly rebut the presumption of credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD explicitly addressed and disagreed with the Applicant's argument about presumption of truthfulness being rebutted on minor inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: The RAD explicitly addressed this issue when it indicated it disagreed with the Applicant’s argument that “[…] the RPD relied in its findings on minor inconsistencies and speculations before deciding that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD explicitly addressed and disagreed with the Applicant's argument on presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: The presumption of truthfulness is rebutted when credibility is fundamentally undermined by inconsistencies and omissions, without explicit statement.
propositions.quote: the presumption of truthfulness is rebutted when a claimant’s credibility is fundamentally undermined by inconsistencies and omissions in both their BOC narrative and oral testimony, without the necessity for the RAD to explicitly state that the presumption has been displaced (Maldonado at page 305; Zerihaymanot v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 610 at para 41).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites authority that the presumption of truthfulness is rebutted by fundamental credibility issues without explicit RAD statement.

propositions.text: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I dismiss the application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance arises for certification, so none is certified.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a serious question of general importance for certification. I am satisfied that none arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question of general importance and declines certification.
